dc.description.abstract.value:
Summary of Indian Stamp Act, 1899
Objective of the Act
The primary objectives of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 are twofold:
1.	Revenue Generation: To generate revenue for the Central and State Governments through the taxation of transactions recorded in documents.
2.	Legal Validity & Evidentiary Value: To impart legal sanction to an instrument. A properly stamped document is considered valid and is admissible as evidence in a court of law.
Key Provisions
1. Definition of "Instrument"
The Act defines an "instrument" as any document by which any right or liability is, or purports to be, created, transferred, limited, extended, extinguished, or recorded. Only the instrument is taxed, not the transaction itself.
2. Chargeability of Stamp Duty
Section 3 of the Act specifies that instruments mentioned in Schedule I (such as Conveyance deeds, Promissory Notes, Bills of Exchange, Lease agreements, etc.) are chargeable with stamp duty. State governments have the power to amend Schedule I, leading to varying stamp duty rates across different states.
3. Types of Stamp Duty
•	Ad Valorem Duty: Calculated as a percentage of the value of the transaction or the property mentioned in the instrument (e.g., Sale Deed, Mortgage).
•	Fixed Duty: A flat rate charged regardless of the transaction value (e.g., Affidavits, Receipts, Adoption Deeds).



4. Timing of Stamping
•	Executed in India: Instruments must be stamped before or at the time of execution (signing).
•	Executed outside India: Instruments executed out of India (except bills of exchange or promissory notes) must be stamped within three months after they are first received in India.
5. Cancellation of Adhesive Stamps
To prevent reuse, the Act mandates that anyone affixing an adhesive stamp to an instrument must cancel it (usually by signing across it or stamping over it). If a stamp is not canceled, the document is legally treated as "unstamped."
6. Consequences of Inadequate or Non-Stamping
•	Inadmissibility as Evidence: An unstamped or inadequately stamped instrument cannot be admitted as evidence in civil courts or acted upon by any public authority.
•	Impounding: Public officers (except police officers) are authorized to impound (confiscate) improperly stamped documents produced before them.
•	Penalties: The defect can often be cured by paying the deficit duty along with a penalty, which can be up to ten times the amount of the deficient duty.
7. Adjudication as to Proper Stamp
If there is doubt about how much duty an instrument requires, a person can apply to the Collector (Section 31) for adjudication. The Collector determines the exact duty payable, providing a certificate that protects the document from future disputes regarding its stamping.
8. Allowances for Spoiled Stamps
The Act provides a mechanism to claim a refund or allowance for stamps that were accidentally spoiled, rendered useless, or not required, provided the application is made within the prescribed time limit (usually six months).

(1) The tuition fees for professional courses such as Engineering & Technology, Medicine, Management, etc., in the university shall be determined by the University under the supervision of the regulatory body notified by the State Government from time to time.
(2) Admission in the University shall be strictly on the basis of merit. Merit for admission in the University may be determined either on the basis of marks or grade obtained in the qualifying examination and achievements in co-curricular and extra-curricular activities or on the basis of marks or grade obtained in the entrance test conducted at State level either by the University or an association of the Universities conducting similar courses or by any agency of the State Government. Provided that the admission in professional educational colleges or institutions of the University shall be governed under the provisions of the Regulatory Bodies.
(3) The university shall allow merit scholarship to at least five percent of the total strength, to the students belonging to poor and economically backward classes. The relevant criteria for determining the poor and economically backward classes shall be such as may be determined by the State Government from time to time.
(4) The university shall compulsorily make provisions for reservation of seats for the students domiciled in the State of Jharkhand to the extent of at least twenty five percent of the total students in the university. The reservation of seats shall be regulated by the laws and orders of the State Government from time to time.
(5) The university shall make provisions for reservation of non-teaching posts in the university for the persons domiciled in the State of Jharkhand to the extent of at least fifty percent of the total number of non-teaching posts of the university. The reservation of seats shall be regulated by the laws and orders of the State Government from time to time.
(6) The university shall appoint adequate number of teachers and officers in the University for maintaining the academic standards specified and shall ensure that the qualifications of such teachers or officers of the university shall not be lower than prescribed by the relevant Regulatory Bodies.
(7) The university shall compulsorily place in the public domain every information in relation to the University which would be of interest to the students and other stakeholders inter alia, including the courses offered , number of seats under different categories, fees and other charges, facilities and amenities offered, faculty in place and such other relevant information.
